title: Master Class | Controlling Center | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: There's nothing wrong with the opponent's reversed-French idea in itself, but this bishop sortie is a mistake — it develops a bishop before a knight and does nothing to stake a claim in the centre. That leaves the door open to seize the middle with tempo.
So grab the centre with gain of time — d5 both plants a pawn in the middle and slaps the bishop, forcing it to react.

The tempting continuation is to keep grabbing space with another pawn, but centre control is a balance — pawns on one hand, and on the other, not overreaching and not neglecting development. Whole openings exist to lure you into overextending until the pawns crumble. So develop instead: the knight to f6 shores up the centre.

The bishop's ideal home is d6 — it braces the e-pawn, and if the opponent castles short it sets up a later pawn thrust with Greek-gift and attacking ideas. But it can't go there just yet, and knowing why is the key.

The obstacle is a capture on d5 winning the pawn — so play c6 first, defending with a pawn, building a chain, and clearing the way for the bishop. A pawn defended by a pawn is always a healthy structure.

And don't fret that c6 takes the natural square from the other knight — the idea that knights must live on c6 and f6 is beginner's lore. Routing a knight to d7 is no tragedy. Those are the conventional posts, usually the best, but chess is a game of trade-offs; a slightly inferior placement doesn't mean a bad position.

The knight leap to g5 looks aggressive but achieves nothing here — its whole purpose is normally to hit f7, and f7 simply isn't a target in this position. There's a solid way to treat it that doesn't even involve reacting.

Rather than shooing the knight, just castle and ignore it. A piece sitting deep in your half isn't automatically a threat — often it's an asset, a stranded horse with nothing to do. Getting the king safe matters more than swatting at a bluff.

Here the intruder becomes an asset. The opponent's central push is premature with pieces scattered — and holding the h-pawn move in reserve pays off, because the moment the knight is finally kicked, the overextended e4-pawn is left attacked twice and defended only once. Reserving that move for the right moment wins more than playing it on reflex.

Don't overthink the recapture — taking the knight to wreck the structure is double-edged, since it also cracks open a file that could rebound. Just take the pawn simply. The wider lesson: when you're agonising over whether to grab a piece, often the best practical answer is to not take it and find a clean alternative, sparing yourself the time and the second-guessing.

That rook move leaves the king stranded in the centre — and notice the whole queenside is still untouched, which means the queen is boxed in with almost no scope. A trapped king and a smothered queen are exactly the cues to pounce on.

The exploitation is straightforward — the bishop swings to g4 and hits the queen, which has no squares to run to. The opponent is reduced to an ugly retreat or a weakening pawn move just to give it air.

If the pawn shields the queen, capture it — the recapture then robs the knight of its own pawn's support, and everything starts to fall. This is all coming from sensible developing moves, no fireworks required.
The queen falls and the game is over — a whole attack built out of nothing but healthy development and centre control.

The takeaway is a picture of two dials: one for controlling the centre with pawns, one for developing the pieces. Miscalibrate them — too little of one, too much of the other — and the position sours. Here too few pawns held the middle while the pieces came out in a rush, so their weight was never felt. Anchoring at least part of the centre with pawns first is what makes the pieces matter.
